summary: Presents a technique to securely provision a networking device that boots in a factory-default state. It can update the boot image, commit an initial configuration, and run scripts, and it works on both public and private networks. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes how a new network device can set itself up without anyone visiting it. The device looks for its instructions on a USB stick, in DNS, over DHCP, or from a server on the network, and it only uses instructions that carry a valid signature from the organisation that owns it.

questions: how does zero touch provisioning work
subtitle: How a factory-fresh network device finds its boot image and configuration on its own, and proves the instructions are genuine.

tldr.problem: Installing a router in a remote branch means sending a specialist to it, which costs money and does not scale. The device needs to be able to bring itself up from nothing but power and a network cable.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines Secure Zero Touch Provisioning: a device asks nearby or remote sources for bootstrapping data, which arrives as signed artifacts containing the boot image, the initial configuration and scripts, and which the device verifies against its own trust anchors before using.
tldr.outcome: The result is that non-technical staff can plug a device in and walk away, while the device still refuses to act on instructions that are not signed by its owner. RFC 8572 is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 9646.

today: RFC 8572 is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 9646; it has not been obsoleted. Anyone implementing SZTP should read the update alongside it.

sections.title: What Secure Zero Touch Provisioning Is
sections.content:
A fundamental business requirement for any network operator is to reduce costs where possible. Deploying devices to many locations can be a significant cost, because sending trained specialists to each site for installations is both cost prohibitive and does not scale.

This document defines Secure Zero Touch Provisioning (SZTP), a bootstrapping strategy that lets devices securely obtain bootstrapping data with no installer action beyond physical placement and connecting the network and power cables. SZTP therefore enables non-technical personnel to bring up devices in remote locations without any operator input.

The solution includes updating the boot image, committing an initial configuration and executing arbitrary scripts to address auxiliary needs. The updated device is subsequently able to establish secure connections with other systems. For instance, a device may establish NETCONF or RESTCONF connections with deployment-specific network management systems.

The document primarily regards physical devices, where the setting of the device's initial state happens during its manufacturing. The solution may be extended to virtual machines or other logical constructs, but the details are left for future work.

Two use cases frame the design. The first is a device connecting to a remotely administered network, such as a remote branch office or convenience store where the device connects as an access gateway to an ISP's network. Assuming it is not possible to customize the ISP's network to provide any bootstrapping support, and with no other nearby device to leverage, the device has no recourse but to reach out to an Internet-based bootstrap server. The second covers a device connecting to a locally administered network: the same, except that the device may additionally leverage nearby devices, which may direct it to a local service to bootstrap from. If no such information is available, or the device cannot use it, it can then reach out to the network just as it would in the first case.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is that someone who is not a network specialist can plug a device into a socket and a network cable, and walk away. The device sorts out the rest for itself, without being trusted to just do whatever it is told.

sections.title: Redirect and Onboarding Information
sections.content:
Two types of conveyed information can be accessed during the bootstrapping process.

Redirect information redirects a device to another bootstrap server. It encodes a list of bootstrap servers, each specifying the server's hostname or IP address, an optional port and an optional trust anchor certificate that the device can use to authenticate that server with. Redirect information may be trusted or untrusted. It is trusted whenever it is obtained via a secure connection to a trusted bootstrap server, or whenever it is signed by the device's owner, and untrusted in all other cases. Trusted redirect information is useful for enabling a device to establish a secure connection to a specified bootstrap server, which is possible when it includes that server's trust anchor certificate. Untrusted redirect information is useful for directing a device to a bootstrap server where signed data has been staged for it to obtain; when the redirect information is untrusted, devices discard any potentially included trust anchor certificates.

Onboarding information provides the data a device needs to bootstrap itself and establish secure connections with other systems. It can specify details about the boot image the device must be running, an initial configuration the device must commit, and scripts that the device must successfully execute. Its data model has a boot-image container, holding an operating system name and version, one or more download URIs, and image-verification entries pairing a hash algorithm with a hash value; and it has a configuration-handling enumeration, a pre-configuration script, the configuration itself and a post-configuration script.

Onboarding information must be trusted for it to be of any use to a device: there is no option for a device to process untrusted onboarding information. It is trusted whenever it is obtained via a secure connection to a trusted bootstrap server, or whenever it is signed by the device's owner.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two kinds of message. One says "go and ask over there", and the other carries the actual instructions: which system software to run, what configuration to commit and what scripts to run.

sections.title: The Three Artifacts
sections.content:
Three artifacts can be made available to devices while they are bootstrapping. The term "artifact" covers all three, and together they provide all the bootstrapping data a device may use.

The conveyed information artifact encodes the essential bootstrapping data for the device, and carries the redirect and onboarding information types. It is a Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) structure encoded using ASN.1 distinguished encoding rules, and its content MUST conform to the YANG module of Section 6.3. The artifact may be signed or unsigned; when signed it may also be encrypted, but it is still signed data. The CMS content type follows the combination: id-data for unsigned and unencrypted content, id-envelopedData for encrypted content, and id-signedData for signed content, with the inner type naming the XML or JSON form of the conveyed information.

The owner certificate is an X.509 certificate that binds an owner identity to a public key, which a device can use to validate a signature over the conveyed information artifact. It may be communicated along with its chain of intermediate certificates leading up to a known trust anchor.

The ownership voucher is the voucher artifact defined in RFC 8366, and it is used to assign a device to an owner.

Each of the three artifacts may be individually encrypted, which may matter where the content is sensitive. They are encrypted in the same way, by the unencrypted form being encapsulated inside a CMS EnvelopedData type. As a consequence, both the conveyed information and the ownership voucher are signed and then encrypted; they are never encrypted and then signed. That sequencing shrouds the signer's certificate and lets the owner be sure what is being signed. It also lets the owner inspect an unencrypted voucher obtained from a manufacturer and encrypt the voucher later, perhaps while also stapling in current revocation objects, when ready to place the artifact in an unsafe location. When encrypted, the CMS MUST be encrypted using a secure device identity certificate for the device, which may be the same as the TLS-level client certificate the device uses when connecting to bootstrap servers.

Only certain groupings of the artifacts make sense. Unsigned Data is useful when transport-level security can convey trust, such as over HTTPS, or when the conveyed information can be processed provisionally. Signed Data without revocations is useful when signed data is needed and revocations either are not needed or can be obtained dynamically. Signed Data with revocations is useful when signed data is needed and revocations are needed but cannot be obtained dynamically. In the unsigned grouping there is no ownership voucher and no owner certificate; in the signed groupings there are, with or without revocations.
sections.plainLanguage: Three pieces are exchanged: the instructions themselves, a certificate that says who signed them, and a voucher that says the device belongs to that owner. The signature is always applied before the encryption, never the other way round.

sections.title: Sources of Bootstrapping Data
sections.content:
Four sources are defined, and the list is not meant to be exhaustive.

A directly attached removable storage device, such as a USB flash drive, MAY be used. Use of removable storage is compelling, because it requires no external infrastructure, and the raw boot image file can also be located on it, making it a fully self-standing bootstrapping solution. The device need only detect that it is plugged in and mount its filesystem. A removable storage device is an untrusted source, so the information stored on it either MUST be signed or MUST be information that can be processed provisionally. Because it presents itself as a filesystem, the artifacts are mapped to files: the conveyed information, the owner certificate and the ownership voucher.

A DNS server MAY be used, which is compelling for deployments that already have DNS infrastructure, because it enables a touchless bootstrapping option that does not entail using an Internet-based resource hosted by a third party. DNS is an untrusted source: even with DNSSEC the device cannot be sure that the domain returned to it belongs to its rightful owner. A device first queries for device-specific records and then, only if that does not bootstrap successfully, for device-independent ones; each query is tried with multicast DNS first and unicast DNS second. Device-specific queries use TXT records under the serial number followed by the globally scoped attribute "_sztp", and device-independent queries use SRV records under the service name "_sztp._tcp". A device-independent response can only carry unsigned data, since signed data needs a device-specific ownership voucher.

A DHCP server MAY be used to hand the device a list of bootstrap servers. The DHCPv4 SZTP Redirect Option has option code 143 and the DHCPv6 option has code 136; both carry a list of bootstrap server URIs, and the URI MUST use the "https" scheme in the form "https://<ip-address-or-hostname>[:<port>]".

A bootstrap server is any RESTCONF server implementing the YANG module of Section 7.3. Using one is a compelling option, because it may use transport-level security, which removes the need for signed data and may be easier to deploy in some environments. The device identifies itself with a TLS-level client certificate or an HTTP authentication scheme, and if both are used they must both identify the same serial number.
sections.plainLanguage: The device looks in four places: a USB stick, the DNS server, the DHCP server, and a bootstrap server on the network. The first three cannot be trusted on their own, so what they hand over has to be signed.

sections.title: The Device Boot Sequence
sections.content:
A device that claims to support this bootstrapping strategy MUST have a particular initial state and boot logic.

The initial state is set during manufacturing. In read/write storage there is a flag that enables SZTP bootstrapping, which MUST be enabled by default so that bootstrapping runs when the device first powers on, and it is a goal that the configuration installed by the bootstrapping process disables it. In read-only storage there are the TLS client certificate and related intermediate certificates, a list of trusted well-known bootstrap servers, a list of trust anchor certificates for bootstrap servers and a list of trust anchor certificates for ownership vouchers. In secure storage there are the private key for the TLS client certificate and the private key for decrypting SZTP artifacts, both of which SHOULD be kept in a cryptographic processor such as a trusted platform module chip.

The boot sequence has four steps. When the device powers on it first checks whether SZTP bootstrapping is configured; if not, it boots normally. It then iterates over its list of sources for bootstrapping data, trying to load data from each. If it manages to bootstrap itself from any of the sources, it runs with the new bootstrapped configuration. Otherwise it MUST loop back through the list again. At any time the device may be configured through an alternate provisioning mechanism, such as a command-line interface, and whatever is used SHOULD unset the flag that enables SZTP bootstrapping.

Processing a source is a recursive algorithm, because a source may return redirect information, which causes the algorithm to run again for the newly discovered sources. An expression that captures all possible successful sequences is: zero or more redirect information responses, followed by one onboarding information response. The algorithm uses a conceptual variable called "trust-state", initialized to FALSE, and the goal is for the device to process onboarding information while trust-state is TRUE. A bootstrap server that the device can authenticate by X.509 certificate path validation to one of its pre-configured trust anchors, or to a trust anchor learned from a previous step, makes trust-state TRUE.

Processing redirect information is straightforward: the device steps through the list of provided bootstrap servers until it finds one it can bootstrap from. If a hostname resolves to more than one address, the device attempts to connect to all of them at least once before moving on. If the redirect information is trusted and the entry carries a trust anchor certificate, the device authenticates that server's TLS certificate to the specified trust anchor; if the entry carries no trust anchor, the device establishes a provisional connection by blindly accepting the server certificate and sets trust-state to FALSE. If the redirect information is untrusted, the device discards any trust anchors it carries and establishes a provisional connection.

Processing onboarding information has a fixed order: the boot image information first, then the pre-configuration script, then the initial configuration, then the post-configuration script. If boot image criteria are specified, the device checks whether it is already running that image; if not, it downloads, verifies and installs the image in that order, and then reboots. It may only use the URIs supplied by the onboarding information, and must verify the image with one of the supplied fingerprints or a signature embedded in the image itself. If an error occurs at any step, the device stops processing and returns to the enclosing loop of the bootstrapping sequence.
sections.plainLanguage: On power-up the device tries each source in turn. If a source only says "go and ask that server instead", the device follows the pointer and tries again. When it finally gets real instructions it installs the software, runs the scripts and commits the configuration, in that order.

sections.title: Checking Signed Data
sections.content:
Whenever a device is presented signed data, it MUST validate it, and that includes the case where the signed data comes from a trusted source. Whenever there is signed data, the device must also be given an ownership voucher and an owner certificate.

The first step is to authenticate the ownership voucher by validating its signature to one of the pre-configured trust anchors, which may entail using additional intermediate certificates attached to the voucher. If the device has an accurate clock, it must verify that the voucher was created in the past, and if the "expires-on" leaf is present, that it has not yet expired. It must verify that the voucher's "assertion" value is acceptable, that the voucher specifies the device's serial number, and, if the "idevid-issuer" leaf is present, that its value is set correctly. If the authentication succeeds, the device extracts the "pinned-domain-cert" node, an X.509 certificate, that is needed to verify the owner certificate in the next step.

The second step is to authenticate the owner certificate by performing X.509 certificate path verification to the trusted certificate extracted from the voucher's pinned-domain-cert node. If the voucher's "domain-cert-revocation-checks" node is set to "true", the device must verify the revocation status of the chain used to sign the owner certificate, and if a suitably fresh revocation status is unattainable, or a certificate is found to have been revoked, it MUST NOT validate the owner certificate.

Finally the device MUST verify that the conveyed information artifact was signed by the validated owner certificate. If any of these steps fail, the device MUST invalidate the signed data and perform no subsequent steps.
sections.plainLanguage: The checks run in order: the voucher proves the device is yours, the owner certificate proves who signed the instructions, and then the instructions themselves must carry that signature. If any check fails, nothing is installed.

sections.title: The Bootstrap Server API and DHCP Options
sections.content:
The bootstrap server exposes a RESTCONF API defined by the YANG module "ietf-sztp-bootstrap-server". It has two RPCs. The "get-bootstrapping-data" RPC takes optional input parameters, including "signed-data-preferred", a hardware model, an operating system name and version and a nonce, and returns an optional reporting level together with the conveyed information and, optionally, the owner certificate and the ownership voucher. The "report-progress" RPC takes a progress type, an optional message, the SSH host keys and the trust anchor certificates, and is only available when the server is acting as an onboarding server.

Two DHCP options carry the same information in different syntax. The DHCPv4 SZTP Redirect Option, option code 143, and the DHCPv6 SZTP Redirect Option, option code 136, both provision the client with one or more URIs for bootstrap servers that can be contacted to attempt further configuration. The bootstrap server list is a list of URIs, each entry prefixed with a two-octet length field.

The RFC also registers the pieces other protocols need. IANA is asked to create the "ietf-sztp-conveyed-info" and "ietf-sztp-bootstrap-server" YANG module names, to register two content types in the SMI Security for S/MIME CMS Content Type registry, to allocate the two DHCP option codes, to register the service name and transport protocol port number for the bootstrap server, and to register the globally scoped DNS node name used for the device-specific queries.
sections.plainLanguage: The server offers one operation, "give me my instructions", and a second one for the device to report progress. The DHCP options simply tell the device which server to ask.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The solution relies on TLS certificates, owner certificates and ownership vouchers, all of which need an accurate clock to be processed correctly, for example to test validity dates and revocation status. Implementations SHOULD ensure devices have an accurate clock when shipped from manufacturing facilities and take steps to prevent clock tampering. If that is not possible, it is RECOMMENDED to disable the aspects of the solution having clock sensitivity, and to assume that TLS certificates, ownership vouchers and owner certificates never expire and are not revocable. Implementations SHOULD NOT rely on NTP for time, as NTP is not a secure protocol.

IDevID certificates are RECOMMENDED, both for the TLS-level client certificate used when connecting to a bootstrap server and for the device identity certificate used by owners when encrypting the artifacts. All trust anchor certificates MUST be protected from external modification, although devices MAY update them through a verifiable process such as a software upgrade using signed software images. The long-lived private keys should be stored so as to resist discovery, such as in a trusted platform module chip.

The document allows a device to blindly authenticate a bootstrap server's TLS certificate, so that redirect information obtained in an unsecured manner can still be used. To compensate, devices connected to an untrusted bootstrap server must assert that the data they download is signed. Because an untrusted server may be under the control of an adversary, devices SHOULD be cautious about the data they send to it. At the TLS layer a client certificate discloses at least the serial number and may disclose the manufacturer, hardware model and public key, and it is RECOMMENDED that secrecy of the network constituency not be relied on for security. At the HTTP layer an authentication scheme discloses at least the serial number and may reveal a secret that only the device is supposed to know, so devices SHOULD NOT use a scheme such as HTTP Basic with an untrusted server that reveals such a secret. At the RESTCONF layer devices use the "get-bootstrapping-data" RPC but not the "report-progress" RPC when connected to an untrusted server, and it is RECOMMENDED that they only pass the "signed-data-preferred" input parameter to such a server.

For devices supporting more than one source of bootstrapping data, no particular sequencing order has to be observed for security reasons, since the solution for each source is considered equally secure. From a privacy perspective, however, it is RECOMMENDED that devices access local sources before accessing remote ones.
sections.plainLanguage: The weak point is the device's own clock: certificates and vouchers have expiry dates, so a device with a wrong clock may accept things it should not, or refuse things it should. The rest of the guidance is about how much a device should reveal to a server it does not yet trust.

viz.caption: THE FOUR SOURCES OF BOOTSTRAPPING DATA

items.title: Removable storage
items.text: A USB stick plugged into the device. Untrusted, so the data must be signed.

items.title: DNS server
items.text: TXT records under the serial number, or SRV records under _sztp._tcp. Untrusted.

items.title: DHCP server
items.text: A redirect option naming bootstrap servers to try. Untrusted.

items.title: Bootstrap server
items.text: A RESTCONF server. Trusted when its certificate validates to a known anchor.
